newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG rebel soldiers say they control defence force.
newsitem.headline: PNG rebel soldiers say they control defence force.

text.p: Rebel Papua New Guinea army officers said on Saturday they controlled the country's defence force and again called on the prime minister to resign by next Tuesday.

As calm returned to the streets of the capital Port Moresby after two days of violence and looting, rebel officers said they had achieved their military objective of ousting African mercenaries from the South Pacific nation.
Rebel leader Major Walter Enuma said it was now up to the public to force Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan to resign by next Tuesday, when parliament resumes ahead of June elections.
Despite the demand for Chan to step down, Enuma said troops would take no action if he refused.
"The defence force does not intend to take any action. We have achieved our military aim, it's up to the public to demonstrate and keep the pressure on the politicians," he said.
Some 48 mercenaries arrived in Johannesburg on Saturday after being thrown out of Papua New Guinea by Enuma on Friday. Another group left earlier in the week.
The leader of the 70-odd mercenaries, former British colonel Tim Spicer, a former top U.N. peacekeeper who also served in the Falkands and Gulf wars, remains in Port Moresby.
Rebel troops on Saturday handed Spicer over to police who charged him with firearm offences before releasing him to British High Commissioner Bob Lowe just after nightfall.
Spicer has been charged with possessing an unlicensed firearm and with possession of ammunition, police told Reuters.
"He was charged with having an unlicensed Russian-made pistol," a police officer said. "He will appear in court on Monday." The charges can carry a jail sentence or fine.
The mercenaries were hired in a US$36 million contract to crush an uprising on copper-rich Bougainville island but were forced out of this South Pacific nation by troops they were meant to have led.

Papua New Guinea's political crisis began on Monday when army commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok demanded Chan quit over his hiring of the mercenaries. He also demanded Spicer and his men be expelled before they could launch a Bougainville assault.
Singirok was fired and replaced by Colonel Alfred Aikung, an army outsider, but retains the loyalty of his troops and officers.
"The acting commander does not have control of the defence force, the prime minister has been misled," Enuma told a news conference at army headquarters, Murray Barracks, on Saturday.
"The acting commander does not have the confidence of the troops. We are in command, we are in control," added Enuma, surrounded by armed troops.
Outside the barracks, Aikung's burnt-out car gave further proof he had no control of the army. Onlookers said soldiers had torched the car.
The car was covered in angry notices. "Graduated from University of Pacific Engineering, majored in corruption, bribes, power-hungry and glory-seeking," said one. "Lest we forget, RIP," read another.
Enuma said Aikung was not under house arrest but was confined to barracks like the rest of the defence force. A government source said Aikung had left the barracks and was in a "safe house".

Singirok's supporters, led by Enuma, have demanded that the former commander be given back his job. Singirok, who was injured trying to rescue a wounded comrade in Bougainville, is immensely popular among the army rank-and-file.

But the rebels appeared on Saturday to have softened their position on his reinstatement. Enuma said troops would return to normal duties if Singirok was reinstated or his chief of staff Colonel Jack Tuat was appointed acting commander.
The demand for Chan and two of his ministers to resign by Tuesday came initially from Singirok on Friday. He said the mercenary contract was unlawful and unconstitutional.
The 10-page contract, marked "strictly confidential", between Papua New Guinea and British-based mercenary firm Sandline International, was handed to reporters by Singirok.
It showed that the mercenaries were not hired just to train troops but to conduct "offensive operations" on Bougainville and recapture a vast copper mine on the island.
Internationally condemned for hiring the mercenaries, Chan had said they would only go to Bougainville as advisers.

An appendix broke down costs into $29 million for equipment and $7.0 million for manpower. The cost for a 45-strong "special forces team" was put at $4.5 million -- or $100,000 per soldier. PNG soldiers earn around $40 a week.
